subject: bio
title: Transport in Plants
subtitle: Xylem, phloem, transpiration and translocation.
concept: Water moves up the plant from roots to leaves by the cohesion-tension mechanism: transpiration pulls water up xylem vessels as a continuous column.
Sucrose and other organic solutes are transported in phloem by mass flow from source to sink.
Transpiration rate is affected by light, temperature, humidity, wind speed, and the number and position of stomata.

notes.heading: Xylem and Water Transport
items: Xylem transports water and mineral ions from roots to aerial parts — one-way flow. Mature xylem vessels are dead cells with no cytoplasm; their lignified walls are waterproof, strengthened, and prevent collapse under the tension generated during transpiration.

Water enters root hair cells by osmosis (soil water has higher Ψ than the cell contents). It crosses the cortex via the apoplast (cell walls, no membranes) or symplast (through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata). At the endodermis, the Casparian strip (suberin) blocks the apoplast pathway — water is forced through the symplast, giving cells control over mineral entry into the xylem.

notes.heading: The Cohesion-Tension Mechanism
items: Transpiration from mesophyll cells creates a water vapour concentration gradient that drives evaporation through stomata. This removes water from the top of the xylem column, creating tension (negative pressure) that pulls the column upward.

Cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) keeps the column intact — water does not break under the tension. Adhesion to xylem walls provides additional support. No ATP is needed — the driving force is evaporation, ultimately powered by the sun.

notes.heading: Phloem and Translocation
items: Phloem transports sucrose (and amino acids) from sources (photosynthesising leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing roots, developing fruits, meristems). Unlike xylem, flow can be bidirectional.
Sieve tube elements (living but without a nucleus) are connected end-to-end through sieve plates. Companion cells (with all organelles) maintain them metabolically via plasmodesmata.

Mass flow hypothesis: at the source, sucrose is actively loaded into phloem → water follows by osmosis → hydrostatic pressure rises and drives a bulk flow of solution toward the sink, where sucrose is unloaded and the process reverses. Evidence: aphid stylus experiments confirm phloem sap exudes under pressure.

notes.heading: Transpiration
items: Rate of transpiration is increased by: higher temperature (more energy for evaporation), lower humidity (steeper water vapour gradient), higher wind speed (removes saturated air), more light (stomata open wider), larger leaf area.
A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot — used as an indirect measure of transpiration (some water is also used for photosynthesis and cell expansion).

definitions.body: The loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata.
The mechanism by which water is pulled up through xylem by the tension created by transpiration, maintained by cohesion between water molecules.
The transport of organic solutes (mainly sucrose) through the phloem from source to sink.
Water movement through plant cell walls without crossing membranes; blocked at the endodermis by the Casparian strip.
An organ that produces or releases sucrose into the phloem (e.g. photosynthesising leaf).
An organ that uses or stores sucrose from the phloem (e.g. growing root tip, developing fruit).

workedExamples.q: Explain how water moves from the soil into the xylem of a root.

steps.text: Soil water has a higher water potential than root hair cell cytoplasm → water enters by osmosis.
Water moves across the cortex via apoplast (through cell walls) and symplast (through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata) pathways down a Ψ gradient.
At the endodermis, the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast pathway → water is forced through the symplast → cell membranes control which minerals enter the xylem.
Water enters xylem vessels (lowest Ψ in root due to mineral accumulation and transpiration pull).

mistakes: Describing phloem as transporting only sugars — it also transports amino acids, hormones and other organic solutes.
Stating xylem cells are living — mature xylem vessels are dead (no cytoplasm or nucleus).
Confusing apoplast (cell wall, no membrane crossing) with symplast (cytoplasm, crosses membranes via plasmodesmata).
tips: A potometer measures water UPTAKE, not transpiration directly — some water is used for photosynthesis/growth.
For the Casparian strip: its role is to force water through the symplast so cells can REGULATE mineral uptake — don't just say 'it blocks water'.
Mass flow evidence: aphid stylus experiment — aphids insert stylets into phloem; sap exudes under pressure, confirming mass flow.

flashcards.a: Transpiration creates tension at the top of the xylem; cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column that is pulled upward.

flashcards.q: What is the role of the Casparian strip?
flashcards.a: A waterproof band in endodermis cell walls that blocks the apoplast pathway, forcing water through the symplast so minerals can be controlled.
Movement of organic solutes (mainly sucrose) through phloem from source to sink by mass flow.

flashcards.q: How does sucrose move from source to phloem (loading)?
flashcards.a: Sucrose is actively transported into phloem companion cells at the source; it lowers Ψ, water enters by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure to drive mass flow.

flashcards.q: Name three factors that increase transpiration rate.
flashcards.a: Higher temperature; lower humidity; higher wind speed; more light (stomata open); larger leaf area (any 3).

flashcards.q: Why do xylem vessels have lignified walls?
flashcards.a: Lignin is waterproof (prevents leakage) and provides structural support, preventing the vessel from collapsing under the tension created during transpiration.

questions.q: What drives water movement up xylem according to cohesion-tension?
opts: Tension created by transpiration + cohesion of water
questions.exp: Transpiration creates a tension (negative pressure) at the top; cohesion holds the water column together — no ATP needed.

questions.q: Where is sucrose loaded into phloem?
questions.exp: Sucrose is actively loaded at the source (e.g. leaf) into sieve tubes, creating a high solute concentration and driving mass flow.

questions.q: What is measured by a potometer?
opts: Rate of water uptake (as a proxy for transpiration)
questions.exp: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot — this is used as an estimate of transpiration rate.

questions.q: What blocks the apoplast pathway in the endodermis?
questions.exp: The Casparian strip is a waterproof band of suberin in endodermis cell walls that blocks the apoplast, forcing water through the symplast.

questions.q: Which cells in phloem have no nucleus at maturity?
questions.exp: Sieve tube elements lose their nucleus (and most organelles) at maturity; they depend on companion cells for metabolic support.

recall: Describe the cohesion-tension mechanism of water transport.
Explain the role of the Casparian strip.
Describe the mass flow hypothesis for phloem translocation.
